kurz: Why six different returns can be reported for the same investment over the same period, depending on the method of calculation.

bloecke.md:
Which percentage is ultimately reported as the return depends on four points: how and over how many periods the average is taken, which capital the figure refers to, whose deposits and withdrawals are counted, and what has already been deducted. Two correct calculations for the same investment can therefore differ by several percentage points. Once the four points are clear, return figures can be compared. Figures that were deliberately made non-comparable then also stand out.

## Arithmetic and geometric mean

A portfolio rises by 50% in the first year and falls by 50% in the second. The average of the two annual returns is zero. The capital has nevertheless shrunk by a quarter, because €10,000 becomes €15,000 and then €7,500.

The cause lies in the type of average. The **arithmetic mean** adds up the annual returns and divides the sum by their number. It indicates what can be expected in a single, randomly selected year. The **geometric mean**, by contrast, gives the constant annual return that would have led from the initial capital to the final capital. Only the geometric mean describes how the money in the portfolio has developed.

bloecke.erklaerung: The geometric mean, also called CAGR, converts the increase in wealth achieved into a steady annual return.
variablen: capital at the end, including reinvested income
bloecke.beispiel: (7,500 / 10,000)^(1/2) - 1 = -13.4% a year. The arithmetic mean, by contrast, is zero.

bloecke.md: The arithmetic mean is always at least as large as the geometric mean. The two are equal only if the return was identical in every period. The gap widens with volatility. For the S&P 500, the arithmetic mean from 1928 to 2025 was 11.86% and the geometric mean 10.02% a year. That is a difference of 1.84 points with a standard deviation of 19.4%. The DAX achieved 11.24% arithmetic and 8.78% geometric from 1988 to 2025. At 2.46 points, the gap is larger because the DAX, with a standard deviation of 22.0%, fluctuates more.

bloecke.titel: Two paths with the same arithmetic mean
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. Both paths have an arithmetic mean of 5%; the geometric mean is 5.0% and 2.0% a year respectively.

bloecke.md: When looking back, only the geometric mean is relevant. The arithmetic mean is an expected value for a single future year and is wrong as a record of the past.

In 98 years of the S&P 500, the annual return was between 8% and 12% only four times: 1968, 1993, 2004 and 2016. The average return is the result of a calculation and does not describe a typical year. A plan based on 8% a year relies on a figure that almost never occurs as an annual return.

## CAGR as the standard for periods of time

The abbreviation CAGR (compound annual growth rate) refers to the geometric mean and is the usual figure in factsheets. The DAX started on 30 December 1987 at 1,000 points and closed 2025 at 24,490 points. Over 38 years, that is 8.78% a year. The figure says nothing about the path in between; it includes 1997 with plus 47.1% just as it includes 2002 with minus 43.9%.

There are two common sources of error with this figure. First, it depends heavily on the start and end points. The MSCI World returned around 7.7% a year in euros from 1970 to 2025. Investors who only came in at the end of 1974 achieved 9.7% up to 2025. The difference of two percentage points is due solely to the choice of starting year. Second, brochures often confuse total return with annual return. “Plus 120% in ten years” sounds like 12% a year but corresponds to 8.2%.

## Time-weighted and money-weighted return

The return of a fund and the return of its investors are two different quantities. The difference follows from the definition and is not a calculation error.

The **time-weighted return** (TWR) splits the period into segments at every deposit and withdrawal date and chains their returns together. Deposits and withdrawals thus drop out of the calculation. The time-weighted return measures the performance of the manager, who has no say over the payments. All factsheets and indices calculate it this way.

The **money-weighted return** (MWR) is the internal rate of return of all payments. Each euro is weighted by how long it was invested. It measures the investor's result, including their decisions about when to pay in and how much.

bloecke.titel: Example portfolio with a later deposit

bloecke.md:
Time-weighted, the result is 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96, that is, minus 4% over two years or minus 2.0% a year. The manager has thus achieved the market return.

On a money-weighted basis, €100,000 of deposits compares with a final value of €81,600. That is a loss of €18,400. The internal rate of return is minus 17.0% a year, because the €90,000, or 90% of the money, was only invested in the loss-making year.

Both figures are correct; they answer different questions.

bloecke.erklaerung: The money-weighted return r is the interest rate at which the sum of all discounted deposits and withdrawals is zero. It can only be calculated iteratively. Spreadsheets provide the IRR or XIRR function for this.
variablen: payment at time t, deposits negative, final value positive

zeilen: What I actually ended up with

bloecke.md:
The gap between the two returns can be measured. In its *Mind the Gap* study, Morningstar compares fund returns and investor returns every year. In the decade to the end of 2025, the funds returned 9.9% a year, while the average dollar invested earned 8.7%. Morningstar attributes the gap of 1.2 percentage points to the timing and size of purchases and sales.

This figure should be read with caution, because part of the gap arises purely from the arithmetic. Investors who pay regularly into a market that rises over the long term have more money invested later than earlier. The returns of the later years therefore carry more weight in their result. If those years were weaker than the earlier ones, investors fall short of the time-weighted index return without having made any mistake. In 2026, the study's calculation method was criticised in the specialist journal *Financial Analysts Journal*. Using the same sample as in the 2025 edition, the authors put the cost of unfavourable timing of purchases and sales at only 0.10% a year. What is certain is that investors on average lag behind the fund return; the exact size of the gap, however, is uncertain.

bloecke.titel: Return figures that cannot be compared
bloecke.md: If a broker reports the portfolio return on a money-weighted basis and the factsheet calculates on a time-weighted basis, the two figures cannot be compared. The conclusion “my ETF has disappointed me by three points” then compares your own savings plan with a lump-sum investment.

## Price return index and total return index

An index may or may not include dividends. The DAX is a **total return index**, in which distributions are notionally reinvested. There is also the DAX price return index, which tracks prices only. Both started on the same day at 1,000 points. At the end of 2025, the total return index stood at 24,490 points and the price return index at 9,175 points. That corresponds to 8.78% versus 6.00% a year. Around 2.8 percentage points a year therefore come from dividends alone.

Internationally, practice is inconsistent. The S&P 500, Euro Stoxx 50 and Nikkei 225 are quoted in the media as price return indices, the DAX as a total return index. The DAX level and the S&P 500 level are therefore two different quantities and cannot be compared directly.

MSCI indices add a third level. *Price* excludes dividends, *Gross Total Return* includes full dividends and *Net Total Return* is calculated after deducting the withholding tax that a foreign fund cannot reclaim. ETFs almost always track the net version. From 2001 to 2025, the MSCI World returned 6.81% gross and 6.26% net a year in euros, a difference of 0.55 percentage points every year. Currency also affects the return. Over the same period, the same gross index returned 7.77% in dollars and 6.81% in euros.

bloecke.unter: All four values describe the same index over the same period; the value after costs is an illustrative calculation with ongoing charges of 1% a year.

bloecke.md:
## From gross return to the amount credited to the portfolio

There are three deductions between the index return and the amount credited to the portfolio. First, there is the non-refundable withholding tax at fund level, which is already included in the net version of the index. Second, there are ongoing fund charges. For a large world ETF, they currently amount to 0.05% to 0.20% a year; for an active equity fund, typically a multiple of that. Third, the investor pays taxes. Capital income is subject to 25% capital income withholding tax (Kapitalertragsteuer) plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge on it, 26.375% in total, and up to 27.995% for those liable to church tax. For an equity fund, the partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) under Section 20 InvStG (Investment Tax Act) reduces the tax base by 30%.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for an investment of €10,000 over one year in an equity ETF with 30% partial exemption, with the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) already used up.

bloecke.md: A gross return of 8.00% thus becomes 5.91%. Just over a quarter of the return is lost before inflation is even taken into account. The withholding tax is unavoidable, the fund charges are largely a matter of choice, and the tax can be deferred. As long as nothing is sold, an accumulating fund incurs no tax apart from the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale); with a distributing fund, the distributions are taxed.

In 2026, the saver's allowance is €1,000 per person, or €2,000 for joint assessment. Without an exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag) at the bank, it is not applied automatically. The tax is then withheld and has to be reclaimed via the capital income annex (Anlage KAP). With several securities accounts, the amount can be split.

## Return figures in advertising

Some of this is regulated by law. Under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565, investment firms must show performance figures over complete twelve-month periods, state the period and the data source, point out any currency risk and make clear that the past is not an indicator of the future. Since the PRIIPs reform, a fund's key information document has contained four scenarios instead of a single figure, together with a statement of how many percentage points the costs reduce the return by.

These requirements prevent false statements. They do not, however, prevent providers from selecting the figures most favourable to them. The following list helps you check a return figure.

1. The start and end points of the period make a difference of several percentage points. The same period must therefore apply to everything being compared, even if a different one would look more favourable.
2. Always convert total returns into an annual return (p.a.). “Plus 120%” over ten years is 8.2% a year.
3. If “average return” appears without further qualification, the arithmetic mean may be meant. It is then legitimate to ask how it was calculated.
4. With the index version, what matters is whether dividends are included and whether the calculation is gross or net. A fund systematically looks worse against a gross index and systematically better against a price return index.
5. Returns in dollars do not reflect what a euro investor has achieved.
6. Backtests and “simulated past performance” are optimised with hindsight. A real fund with a five-year history says more than a backtest over thirty years.
7. Qualifications such as “up to”, an introductory rate for new customers for three months or a return before the initial charge are in the footnote, while the figure is in the headline.

bloecke.titel: Quick check of a return figure
bloecke.md: For any return figure, the period, currency and deductions should be known, as well as who decided on the timing of payments. If any of this information is missing, that in itself is a warning sign.

mitnehmen: When looking back, only the geometric mean counts, because the arithmetic mean overstates the result all the more, the greater the fluctuations were.
The time-weighted return measures the manager, the money-weighted return the investor, which is why the same investment can have returned minus 2% and minus 17% a year.
The DAX includes dividends, most other well-known index levels do not; for the DAX, this difference amounts to around 2.8 percentage points a year.
In the illustrative calculation, around 5.9% of an 8% gross return remains after withholding tax, fund charges and flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer).
A return figure is only usable with four pieces of information: period, currency, calculation method and deductions.

begriffe.text: The constant annual return that would have led from the initial capital to the final capital. For looking back, it is the only valid measure.
Abbreviation of compound annual growth rate, another name for the geometric mean of the annual returns.
Chaining of the period returns, independent of deposits and withdrawals. It measures the performance of the manager and is abbreviated to TWR.
The internal rate of return of all payments. It weights each euro by how long it was invested, measures the investor's result and is abbreviated to MWR.
An index that notionally reinvests dividends, for example the DAX. A price return index does not take dividends into account.
A flat-rate reduction of a fund's taxable income, 30% for equity funds held as private assets (Section 20 InvStG).
